what: The sections of this article, each with a line and a paragraph, for showing what the reader has already read. Built by admin/build/summaries.py from admin/content/articles/summaries/.

sections.label: The opening
sections.line: I miss a feature, which means the newsroom works
sections.para: I read the newsroom on four devices and they disagree, because everything lives in each browser. Missing a feature is the best signal: builders who use their product find its direction, and the loop from comment to feature is the moat. The article ends with a brief for the reader's own encrypted vault.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Builders must use their product; usage gives direction
sections.para: The people who set the roadmap must be users, as at Apple. I failed this with The Cyber Boardroom, MyFeeds and early sgit; vaults pass it, with 54 published here. Agents can build anything, so direction is scarce, and a fast loop, 81 minutes from brief to live, is the moat.

sections.label: The people who decide the roadmap have to use it
sections.line: Makers who use their product feel friction first
sections.para: Everyone stresses user connection, but the key users are those building the product and controlling the roadmap. Daily use on real work shortens the loop, surfaces unplanned uses and shows which next feature hurts, which I think explains Apple. When a team uses something else, the product is weaker than it looks.

sections.label: The brutal part
sections.line: I never used my past startups: the signal
sections.para: The Cyber Boardroom, MyFeeds and early sgit were good ideas, but I was not using them, and that meant something was missing. Vaults are the opposite: I and my agents create them constantly, and 54 are published here with read keys. They improve because daily use drives each release.

sections.label: Direction is the scarce part
sections.line: Agents can build anything; usage supplies the direction
sections.para: A model that can go in every direction needs someone with a direction, as argued in two earlier articles. Agents cannot generate what to build next, for whom, or when to stop, and context comes most reliably from use. Missing a feature is the product saying where it wants to go.

sections.label: The loop is the moat
sections.line: Shipping speed, not technology, is the defensible moat
sections.para: Earlier I wrote that the moat is data, relationships, distribution or speed of shipping, and this week made speed concrete. A comment leads to an article, then a shipped feature I use. A personal reading list went from brief to live in 81 minutes, a persona link in 17 hours.

sections.label: Part two: the brief for the feature I miss
sections.line: Brief: a per-reader encrypted vault syncing every device
sections.para: The brief asks for a reader vault holding personas, history, lists, ratings and receipts, with no server database or password. It uses an access key, a Web Crypto key pair under RFC 0001, one append-only log per device merged by union, a scan-to-add-device flow, and encrypted one-way notes to the site agent.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.line: One user is a direction, not proof of demand
sections.para: I am the first user and best placed to feel the gap, but that is not proof others want it; other and synthetic readers will tell. Not using my earlier startups is one reason among several they failed. None of the vault feature is built yet: the brief is a design.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.line: Sources: my memo, git logs and related articles
sections.para: Based on my voice memo of 11 October 2026 after reading on four devices; figure balances are illustrative, times come from the site and newsroom git logs. Related pieces include whether they miss it, Knowing when to stop, From me to you, in a link, No server, by design, and RFC 0001.
